standing_assumptions:
The work is a four-page note (Journal of Causal Inference, DOI 10.1515/jci-2016-0007) in an online-first layout: no page numbers are printed, so every location below is a PDF page. It contains one assumption, two definitions, four propositions and one corollary, all on PDF pp. 1-3; there is no appendix, supplement or code. Everything quoted below was read from the rendered page images.
[S1. Population and effects: Section 2, first paragraph, PDF p. 1] “Consider a full data probability distribution $G$ with an associated causal effect distribution $\tau$ with finite expectation $\mathrm{E}_G[\tau]$, where $\mathrm{E}_G[.]$ denotes the expectation over the distribution $G$. Further denote the support of the distribution of $\tau$ as $\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau]$. We impose a regularity condition on $\tau$ establishing non-degeneracy of $\tau$.”
[S2. Assumption 1: PDF p. 1] “Assumption 1: (Effect heterogeneity). $\min\left(\sup\left(\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau]\right) - \mathrm{E}_G[\tau], \mathrm{E}_G[\tau] - \inf\left(\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau]\right)\right) = c > 0$.” Followed by: “Assumption 1 is equivalent to assuming that causal effects are not constant across observations in the distribution $G$; i.e., causal effects are heterogeneous.”
[S3. Data and estimator: PDF p. 1] “We do not observe the full data probability distribution $G$, but we observe an empirical distribution $F_n$. Suppose that, using $F_n$, we have a root-n consistent and asymptotically normal estimator of the average causal effect $\mathrm{E}_G[\tau]$, $\hat\theta$.”
[S4. Definition 1: PDF p. 2] “Definition 1: An estimator $\hat\theta$ is root-n consistent and asymptotically normal for $\theta_0$ if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta_0) = N(0, \sigma^2) + o_p(1)$, for some $0 < \sigma^2 < \infty$.”
[S5. Definition 2: PDF p. 2] “We now define the target parameter, $\theta_{F_n}$.” “Definition 2: Let the target parameter $$\theta_{F_n} = \begin{cases} \hat\theta & : |\hat\theta - \mathrm{E}_G[\tau]| \le c \\ \mathrm{E}_G[\tau] + c & : \hat\theta - \mathrm{E}_G[\tau] > c \\ \mathrm{E}_G[\tau] - c & : \hat\theta - \mathrm{E}_G[\tau] < -c \end{cases},$$ where, as in Assumption 1, $c = \min\left(\sup\left(\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau]\right) - \mathrm{E}_G[\tau], \mathrm{E}_G[\tau] - \inf\left(\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau]\right)\right)$.” Followed by: “The target parameter adapts naturally to the closest value in an interval surrounding $\mathrm{E}_G[\tau]$, where the width of the interval is defined by the support of $\tau$. We formalize how each $\theta_{F_n}$ is a local average treatment effect.”
[Which hypotheses each printed result names] Proposition 1 names none (it inherits S1, S3 and Definition 2). Proposition 2 assumes only that $\hat\theta$ is root-n consistent and asymptotically normal for $\mathrm{E}_G[\tau]$; it does not name Assumption 1. Propositions 3 and 4 assume Assumption 1; Proposition 4 replaces Definition 1 by its own condition on $\hat\theta$. Corollary 1 names only its own support condition.
[What the paper does not print; the readings below are those of the audit’s validators, not the paper’s] (i) The sampling scheme that produces $F_n$ and the probability space on which $\hat\theta$ is defined are not specified (PDF p. 1 says only “we observe an empirical distribution $F_n$”). $\Pr$ and the unsubscripted $\mathrm{E}$ in Propositions 3-4 and Corollary 1 are read as the sampling distribution of $\hat\theta$ induced by $G$. The index $n$ on $\hat\theta$, $\tilde\theta$, $u$ and $\varepsilon$ is suppressed in the paper. (ii) “Support” is read as the closed support of the law of $\tau$; only its infimum $L$ and supremum $U$ (the essential infimum and supremum, possibly $-\infty$ and $+\infty$) enter. $c = +\infty$ is allowed (support unbounded in both directions), and then $\theta_{F_n} = \hat\theta$. For $\tau$ with finite mean, Assumption 1 holds if and only if $\tau$ is not almost surely constant. (iii) Definition 2 says that $\theta_{F_n}$ is $\hat\theta$ clipped to $[\mathrm{E}_G[\tau] - c, \mathrm{E}_G[\tau] + c]$: with $\mu = \mathrm{E}_G[\tau]$ and $C(x) = \min(\mu + c, \max(\mu - c, x))$, $\theta_{F_n} = C(\hat\theta)$; the targets also write $r(x) = x - C(x)$, so that $\hat\theta - \theta_{F_n} = r(\hat\theta)$. (iv) “Nonnegative weighting” (Proposition 1) is not defined; it is read as a measurable function $w \ge 0$ on the full-data population with $0 < \mathrm{E}_G[w] < \infty$ and $\mathrm{E}_G[|w\tau|] < \infty$, which may depend on every full-data variable and on the realized $F_n$. (v) The equation in Definition 1 is read as convergence in distribution of $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \theta_0)$ to $N(0, \sigma^2)$, or, in the form the printed proof of Proposition 3 uses, as $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \theta_0) = Z_n + R_n$ with $Z_n \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$ and $R_n \to 0$ in probability. The witnesses in P017-T5, P017-T6 and P017-T12 satisfy the second form with an exactly normal $Z_n$; the witness in P017-T1 satisfies the first by the central limit theorem for independent, identically distributed, bounded summands. In Proposition 4, “$N(0, \sigma^2) + \varepsilon$” is read as $Z_n + \varepsilon_n$ with $Z_n \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$ and no independence assumed between $Z_n$ and $\varepsilon_n$.
[Why the list has these targets] Four findings rated as errors concern a mathematical statement: P017-E001 (Moderate: Proposition 1 and the fact cited as its proof), P017-E002 (Moderate: steps in the printed proofs of Propositions 3 and 4), P017-E004 (Minor: the probability printed as 0 in the proof of Corollary 1, and the missing differential in the display of the proof of Proposition 4) and P017-N001 (Minor: the word “quickly” after Proposition 3, an overstatement that the validator settled with an exact counterexample). Each has a corrected-statement target, and a counterexample target where a validator gave one. Not targets: P017-E003 (rated a clarity note; its repair of the same sentence is quoted in P017-T13), P017-N002 (not confirmed), P017-N003 (bibliographic misprints), and headline claim P017-H6 (an interpretive remark in the Discussion). Headline claims H2, H1 and H4 are Propositions 1, 3 and 4, which findings P017-E001 and P017-E002 touch (P017-T9, P017-T14, P017-T15). H3 is Proposition 2 (P017-T16). The mathematical content of H5 is Corollary 1 (P017-T10) and the every-positive-sequence form of Proposition 3 (P017-T7).

canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 2 (no page number is printed); Assumption 1 on PDF p. 1
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement: PDF p. 2] “Proposition 1: There exists a nonnegative weighting associated with each empirical distribution $F_n$, $w_{F_n}$, such that across all $F_n$, $\theta_{F_n} = \frac{\mathrm{E}_G[w_{F_n}\tau]}{\mathrm{E}_G[w_{F_n}]}$.” “A proof of Proposition 1 follows directly from the fact that a weighted mean can obtain any value in the interval defined by the infimum and supremum of its distribution’s support.”
[Counterexample from the validator (v1 derivation.md, section 3); not in the paper.] Full-data law $G$: $\tau \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$, $\Pr(B = -1) = \Pr(B = 1) = \tfrac12$, $T \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\tfrac12)$, mutually independent; potential outcomes $Y(0) = B$ and $Y(1) = B + \tau$, so the unit causal effect is $Y(1) - Y(0) = \tau$; observed data $(T, Y)$ with $Y = T\,Y(1) + (1 - T)\,Y(0)$. Units $i = 1, \ldots, n$ are drawn independently from $G$, and $F_n$ is the empirical distribution of the observed pairs $(T_i, Y_i)$. Estimator (inverse-probability weighting with the known assignment probability $\tfrac12$): $$\hat\theta_n = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i, \qquad X_i = 2T_iY_i - 2(1 - T_i)Y_i.$$
Claims. (a) Population: $\mathrm{E}_G[\tau] = \tfrac12$; $\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau] = [0, 1]$, so $\inf\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau] = 0$, $\sup\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau] = 1$ and $c = \min(1 - \tfrac12, \tfrac12 - 0) = \tfrac12 > 0$ (Assumption 1 holds); $\Pr_G(\tau = 0) = \Pr_G(\tau = 1) = 0$ and $0 < \tau < 1$ almost surely. (b) Estimator: $|X_i| < 4$, $\mathrm{E}[X_i] = \tfrac12$, $\mathrm{E}[X_i^2] = \tfrac{14}{3}$, $\mathrm{Var}(X_i) = \tfrac{53}{12}$; hence $\mathrm{E}[\hat\theta_n] = \tfrac12$, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_n) = \tfrac{53}{12n}$, and $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \tfrac12)$ converges in distribution to $N(0, \tfrac{53}{12})$, so that $\hat\theta_n$ is root-n consistent and asymptotically normal for $\mathrm{E}_G[\tau]$ in the sense of Definition 1 with $\sigma^2 = \tfrac{53}{12}$. (c) Bad realization: for every $n \ge 1$ the event $E_n = \{B_i = -1 \text{ and } T_i = 0 \text{ for all } i \le n\}$ has probability $4^{-n} > 0$; on $E_n$ every $X_i = 2$, so $\hat\theta_n = 2$, $\hat\theta_n - \mathrm{E}_G[\tau] = \tfrac32 > c$, and Definition 2 gives $\theta_{F_n} = \mathrm{E}_G[\tau] + c = 1$; on $E_n$ the empirical distribution $F_n$ is the point mass at $(T, Y) = (0, -1)$. (d) Obstruction: for every function $w$ on the full-data space that is measurable, nonnegative and has $0 < \mathrm{E}_G[w] < \infty$, $$0 < \frac{\mathrm{E}_G[w\tau]}{\mathrm{E}_G[w]} < 1.$$ (e) Consequently, on $E_n$ there is no nonnegative weighting $w$ with $\theta_{F_n} = \mathrm{E}_G[w\tau]/\mathrm{E}_G[w]$: Proposition 1 fails on an event of positive probability for every $n \ge 1$. The cited fact fails as well: $1$ lies in the interval $[0, 1]$ defined by the infimum and supremum of the support of $\tau$, and no weighted mean of $\tau$ equals $1$. (f) Lower endpoint, same law: on $\{B_i = 1 \text{ and } T_i = 0 \text{ for all } i \le n\}$ (probability $4^{-n}$, disjoint from $E_n$) every $X_i = -2$, so $\hat\theta_n = -2$ and $\theta_{F_n} = \mathrm{E}_G[\tau] - c = 0$, which by (d) no nonnegative weighting attains.

[Not in the paper; defined by the validator, v1 derivation.md section 3] the joint law of $(\tau, B, T)$, the potential outcomes, the observed pair $(T, Y)$, the estimator $\hat\theta_n$ (defined also on samples with no treated unit, because it uses the known probability $\tfrac12$ and no empirical denominator) and the events in (c) and (f). Conditional on $(B, T)$, each of the four cases has probability $\tfrac14$: $(B, T) = (-1, 0)$ gives $X = 2$; $(-1, 1)$ gives $X = -2 + 2\tau$; $(1, 0)$ gives $X = -2$; $(1, 1)$ gives $X = 2 + 2\tau$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: The counterexample is exact for each fixed $n$. Its one limit statement is the last clause of (b), which checks that the witness estimator satisfies the hypothesis “root-n consistent and asymptotically normal”; the exact facts it rests on are that the $X_i$ are independent and identically distributed with $|X_i| < 4$, $\mathrm{E}[X_i] = \tfrac12$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X_i) = \tfrac{53}{12} \in (0, \infty)$, and that $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_n) = \tfrac{53}{12n}$ (Chebyshev’s inequality then gives consistency). The conditional second moments are $4$, $\tfrac43$, $4$ and $\tfrac{28}{3}$ in the order of the four cases listed under definitions_needed.
canonical_claim.note: P017-E001 is rated an error, Moderate (ratings.json), so this target and P017-T2 to P017-T4 have priority 2. Two validators confirmed the finding, each with a Lean proof, and both re-runs upheld the verdicts. The target is the first validator’s construction. It does not formalize the joint law of $(\tau, B, T)$, the estimator, the event $E_n$ or the limit in (b); those are in derivation.md section 3 and in exact_check.py (rational and symbolic arithmetic, no simulation). The second validator gave an independent witness with countably many atoms (runs/P017/validate/P017-E001/v2/artifact/derivation.md, sections 2-3, and check.lean): $\Pr(K = k) = 2^{-k}$ for $k \ge 1$; $S = \pm 1$, $B = \pm 2$ and $T \in \{0, 1\}$ equiprobable; all four independent; $\tau = S(1 - 2^{-K})$, $Y(0) = B$, $Y(1) = B + \tau$. There $\mathrm{E}_G[\tau] = 0$, the support has infimum $-1$ and supremum $1$ with no mass at either, $c = 1$, the same estimator has $\mathrm{Var}(X_i) = \tfrac{356}{21}$, and on the event that every unit has $K = 1$, $S = 1$, $B = 2$, $T = 1$ (probability $16^{-n}$) $\hat\theta_n = 5$ and $\theta_{F_n} = 1$, while every admissible weighted mean lies strictly between $-1$ and $1$. It is recorded for reference and is not a separate target. What the counterexample does not show: any failure of the numerical conclusions of Propositions 2-4 or of Corollary 1, or any failure of Proposition 1 when $\tau$ has finite support or support unbounded in both directions. The corrected statements are P017-T2 (the cited fact), P017-T3 (Proposition 1 with Definition 2 unchanged) and P017-T4 (Proposition 1 with a smaller clipping radius).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The fact cited as the proof of Proposition 1, as corrected (which values a nonnegatively weighted mean attains)
canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 2 (no page number is printed)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed: PDF p. 2] “A proof of Proposition 1 follows directly from the fact that a weighted mean can obtain any value in the interval defined by the infimum and supremum of its distribution’s support.”
[Correction. Sol’s smallest_repair for P017-E001 (validated.json): “Replace the proof fact by the same interior-plus-endpoint-atoms statement.” Sol’s corrected text: “A weighted mean attains every finite value strictly between the effect-support bounds, and attains a finite endpoint if and only if the endpoint has positive probability.” Written out from the validators’ derivations (v1 section 2; v2 section 4).]
Corrected fact in full. Let $\tau$ be a real random variable on the full-data probability space with law $G$ and $\mathrm{E}_G[|\tau|] < \infty$, and let $t \in \mathbb{R}$. Call a function $w$ on that space an admissible weighting if it is measurable, $w \ge 0$, $0 < \mathrm{E}_G[w] < \infty$ and $\mathrm{E}_G[|w\tau|] < \infty$. Then there exists an admissible weighting $w$ with $$\frac{\mathrm{E}_G[w\tau]}{\mathrm{E}_G[w]} = t$$ if and only if $$\Pr\nolimits_G(\tau = t) > 0 \quad\text{or}\quad \bigl(\Pr\nolimits_G(\tau < t) > 0 \text{ and } \Pr\nolimits_G(\tau > t) > 0\bigr).$$
Consequences, with $L = \inf\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau]$ and $U = \sup\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau]$ (possibly $-\infty$ and $+\infty$): (i) every real $t$ with $L < t < U$ is attained; (ii) a finite endpoint $t \in \{L, U\}$ is attained if and only if $\Pr_G(\tau = t) > 0$; (iii) no $t < L$ and no $t > U$ is attained.
Explicit weights for the “if” direction. If $p_0 = \Pr_G(\tau = t) > 0$: $w = \mathbf{1}\{\tau = t\}/p_0$. If $p_- = \Pr_G(\tau < t) > 0$ and $p_+ = \Pr_G(\tau > t) > 0$: with $m_- = \mathrm{E}_G[\tau\mathbf{1}\{\tau < t\}]/p_-$ and $m_+ = \mathrm{E}_G[\tau\mathbf{1}\{\tau > t\}]/p_+$ one has $m_- < t < m_+$, and with $a = (m_+ - t)/(m_+ - m_-) \in (0, 1)$, $$w = \frac{a}{p_-}\mathbf{1}\{\tau < t\} + \frac{1 - a}{p_+}\mathbf{1}\{\tau > t\}.$$ In both cases $w$ is bounded and nonnegative, $\mathrm{E}_G[w] = 1$ and $\mathrm{E}_G[w\tau] = t$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Effect distribution and support: Section 2, first paragraph, PDF p. 1] $\tau$ has finite expectation under $G$; $\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau]$ is the support of its distribution. [Weighted mean] The paper’s expression is $\mathrm{E}_G[w\tau]/\mathrm{E}_G[w]$ (Proposition 1, PDF p. 2). [Nonnegative weighting] Not defined in the paper; read by the validators as a function $w$ on the full-data population that is measurable, $w \ge 0$, $0 < \mathrm{E}_G[w] < \infty$ and $\mathrm{E}_G[|w\tau|] < \infty$, allowed to depend on every full-data variable and on the realized $F_n$ (standing assumption (iv)). [Not in the paper] the two-sided condition, $p_0$, $p_\pm$, $m_\pm$ and $a$ are the validators’ (v1 derivation.md section 2).
canonical_claim.note: The printed fact is false at a support endpoint that carries no probability (P017-T1). The correction is an exact statement about one integrable random variable; no sample, estimator or limit is involved. The weight is allowed to depend on all full-data variables, not on $\tau$ alone. “Only if”, as the validators argue it: if $\Pr_G(\tau = t) = 0$ and $\Pr_G(\tau < t) = 0$ then $\tau > t$ almost surely, and $\mathrm{E}_G[w\tau] = t\,\mathrm{E}_G[w]$ would give $\mathrm{E}_G[w(\tau - t)] = 0$ with a nonnegative integrand, hence $w = 0$ almost surely, contradicting $\mathrm{E}_G[w] > 0$; symmetrically on the other side. The upper-endpoint case of this direction (if $\tau < 1$ almost everywhere then the weighted mean is $< 1$) is the Lean theorem unattainable_upper_endpoint in runs/P017/validate/P017-E001/v1/artifact/check.lean; the “if” direction and the two-sided statement are not in Lean. Consequences (i)-(iii) use only that each of $\{\tau < t\}$ and $\{\tau > t\}$ has positive probability when $L < t < U$, and that $\{\tau < L\}$ and $\{\tau > U\}$ are null.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 1, as corrected with Definition 2 unchanged (the representation holds except at a support endpoint without mass, hence with probability tending to one)
canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 2 (no page number is printed)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed: PDF p. 2] “Proposition 1: There exists a nonnegative weighting associated with each empirical distribution $F_n$, $w_{F_n}$, such that across all $F_n$, $\theta_{F_n} = \frac{\mathrm{E}_G[w_{F_n}\tau]}{\mathrm{E}_G[w_{F_n}]}$.” “Proposition 1 asserts that across all realizations, the target parameter $\theta_{F_n}$ corresponds to an average causal effect for at least one subpopulation.”
[Correction. Sol’s smallest_repair for P017-E001 (validated.json), first part: “Leave Definition 2 unchanged and qualify Proposition 1 and its gloss: the representation holds for realizations whose target is strictly between the effect-support bounds, and at a finite endpoint only if that endpoint has positive mass. Under the standing consistency and heterogeneity assumptions it consequently holds with probability tending to one.”]
Corrected proposition in full. Let $G$ be such that $\mathrm{E}_G[|\tau|] < \infty$; write $\mu = \mathrm{E}_G[\tau]$, $L = \inf\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau]$, $U = \sup\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau]$; let Assumption 1 hold, $c = \min(U - \mu, \mu - L) > 0$; and let $\theta_{F_n}$ be as in Definition 2. (a) For every $n$ and every empirical distribution $F_n$ (every realization) such that $L < \theta_{F_n} < U$, or such that $\theta_{F_n}$ is a finite endpoint of the support ($\theta_{F_n} \in \{L, U\}$) with $\Pr_G(\tau = \theta_{F_n}) > 0$, there exists a nonnegative weighting $w_{F_n}$ (measurable, $w_{F_n} \ge 0$, $0 < \mathrm{E}_G[w_{F_n}] < \infty$ and $\mathrm{E}_G[|w_{F_n}\tau|] < \infty$) with $$\theta_{F_n} = \frac{\mathrm{E}_G[w_{F_n}\tau]}{\mathrm{E}_G[w_{F_n}]}.$$ Since $\theta_{F_n}$ always lies in $[L, U]$, the only remaining case is that $\theta_{F_n}$ is a finite endpoint of the support with $\Pr_G(\tau = \theta_{F_n}) = 0$, and in that case no such weighting exists. (b) In particular the representation exists on every realization with $|\hat\theta - \mathrm{E}_G[\tau]| < c$ (there $\theta_{F_n} = \hat\theta$ and $L \le \mu - c < \hat\theta < \mu + c \le U$). It exists on every realization whatsoever if $c = +\infty$ (support unbounded in both directions), or if each of the two values $\mu - c$, $\mu + c$ that is an endpoint of the support has positive probability under $G$ (for example, if $\tau$ takes finitely many values). (c) If in addition $\hat\theta$ is root-n consistent and asymptotically normal for $\mathrm{E}_G[\tau]$ (Definition 1), then $\Pr(|\hat\theta_n - \mathrm{E}_G[\tau]| < c) \to 1$ as $n \to \infty$, so the probability that $\theta_{F_n}$ is a nonnegatively weighted mean of $\tau$ tends to one. The gloss is corrected in the same way: the target parameter corresponds to an average causal effect for at least one subpopulation on the realizations described in (a), not “across all realizations”.

canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 2 (no page number is printed)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Correction. Sol’s corrected text for P017-E001 (validated.json, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim: “Let mu=E_G[tau] and choose a fixed finite radius 0<d<c. Define theta^(d)_{F_n}=clip_[mu-d,mu+d](theta_hat). For every empirical distribution F_n, this target is an ordinary nonnegative weighted average of the full-data causal effects. A weighted mean attains every finite value strictly between the effect-support bounds, and attains a finite endpoint if and only if the endpoint has positive probability. canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed: proof of Proposition 3, PDF p. 2] “Decompose $\hat\theta$ into $\tilde\theta = N(\mathrm{E}_G[\tau], \sigma^2/n)$ and $u = o_p(n^{-1/2})$, so that $\hat\theta = \tilde\theta + u$. Since $(\tilde\theta - \theta_{F_n})$ is $o_p(a_n)$ for any positive sequence $(a_n)$, the rate of convergence of $\hat\theta$ is at worst governed by the bound ensured by $u$’s $o_p(n^{-1/2})$ convergence. To prove the claim, note that for any positive $\varepsilon$, $\Pr\left(\frac{|\tilde\theta - \theta_{F_n}|}{a_n} \ge \varepsilon\right) \le \Pr\left(\tilde\theta - \theta_{F_n} \ne 0\right) = 2\Phi(-c\sqrt{n}/\sigma)$, where $\Phi(.)$ denotes the standard Normal CDF. Since $\lim_{n\to\infty} 2\Phi(-c\sqrt{n}/\sigma) = 0$, $(\tilde\theta - \theta_{F_n})$ is $o_p(a_n)$.”
[Counterexample from the validator (derivation.md, sections 2-4); not in the paper.] Model: for each unit independently, $X_i \sim N(\mu, 1)$ and $R_i$ uniform on $\{-1, 1\}$, independent of each other; potential outcomes $Y_i(0) = 0$ and $Y_i(1) = \mu + R_i$, so $\tau_i = \mu + R_i$; the observed empirical distribution $F_n$ contains the $X_i$. Evaluate at $\mu = 0$. Then $\mathrm{E}_G[\tau] = 0$, $\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau] = \{-1, 1\}$ and $c = 1$, so Assumption 1 holds. Put $$\tilde\theta_n = \bar X_n, \qquad u_n = \frac1n, \qquad \hat\theta_n = \bar X_n + \frac1n.$$ Then $\tilde\theta_n \sim N(0, 1/n)$ exactly (so $\sigma = 1$), $\sqrt{n}\,u_n = n^{-1/2} \to 0$ (so $u_n = o_p(n^{-1/2})$), and $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \mathrm{E}_G[\tau]) = Z_n + n^{-1/2}$ with $Z_n = \sqrt{n}\,\bar X_n \sim N(0, 1)$: $\hat\theta_n$ is root-n consistent and asymptotically normal for $\mathrm{E}_G[\tau]$ (Definition 1), and $\hat\theta_n = \tilde\theta_n + u_n$ is the decomposition of the printed proof. By Definition 2, $\theta_{F_n} = \max(-1, \min(1, \hat\theta_n))$.
Claims. Write $D_n = \tilde\theta_n - \theta_{F_n}$ and $x = \tilde\theta_n$. (a) Exact form, for every $n \ge 1$: $D_n = x + 1$ if $x < -1 - \tfrac1n$; $D_n = -\tfrac1n$ if $-1 - \tfrac1n \le x \le 1 - \tfrac1n$; $D_n = x - 1$ if $x > 1 - \tfrac1n$. (b) Hence $D_n = 0$ only when $\tilde\theta_n = 1$, an event of probability zero, and $$\Pr(\tilde\theta_n - \theta_{F_n} \ne 0) = 1 \quad\text{for every } n \ge 1,$$ whereas the printed value is $2\Phi(-c\sqrt{n}/\sigma) = 2\Phi(-\sqrt{n}) = \Pr(|\tilde\theta_n| > 1)$, which is $< 1$ for every $n \ge 1$ and $\le \tfrac1n$ by Chebyshev’s inequality (for instance $2\Phi(-5) \le \tfrac1{25}$ at $n = 25$). The printed equality is false. (c) Take the positive sequence $a_n = 1/n$. For $n \ge 2$, on $A_n = \{|\tilde\theta_n| \le \tfrac12\}$ one has $D_n = -\tfrac1n$, and $\Pr(A_n) \ge 1 - \tfrac4n$. Hence $\Pr\left(|D_n|/a_n \ge \tfrac12\right) \ge 1 - \tfrac4n \to 1$ and $nD_n \to -1$ in probability, so $(\tilde\theta_n - \theta_{F_n})$ is not $o_p(a_n)$: the printed claim “for any positive sequence $(a_n)$” is false. (d) Proposition 3 itself is not contradicted: $\hat\theta_n - \theta_{F_n} = 0$ on $\{|\hat\theta_n| \le 1\} \supseteq A_n$ for $n \ge 2$.

canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed: proof of Proposition 4, PDF p. 3] “To obtain the rate of convergence of the mean square error of $\tilde\theta$, we integrate over its squared deviation from the target parameter. To ease calculations, we obtain an upper bound by integrating over the squared deviation from $\mathrm{E}_G[\tau]$, rather than from $\theta_{F_n}$: $$\mathrm{E}_G[(\tilde\theta - \theta_{F_n})^2] \le 2\int_c^\infty x^2 \frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{x^2 n}{2\sigma^2}} = c\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\frac{e^{-\frac{c^2 n}{2\sigma^2}}}{\sqrt{n}} + 2\sigma^2\frac{\Phi\left(\frac{-c\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\right)}{n} = o(n^{-1}).$$” (The integral is printed without a differential; it is read with $dx$, see P017-T11.)
[Counterexample from the validator (derivation.md, sections 2, 3 and 5); not in the paper.] The model of P017-T5, repeated here. Model: for each unit independently, $X_i \sim N(\mu, 1)$ and $R_i$ uniform on $\{-1, 1\}$, independent of each other; potential outcomes $Y_i(0) = 0$ and $Y_i(1) = \mu + R_i$, so $\tau_i = \mu + R_i$; the observed empirical distribution $F_n$ contains the $X_i$. Evaluate at $\mu = 0$. Then $\mathrm{E}_G[\tau] = 0$, $\mathrm{Supp}_G[\tau] = \{-1, 1\}$ and $c = 1$, so Assumption 1 holds. Put $$\tilde\theta_n = \bar X_n, \qquad u_n = \frac1n, \qquad \hat\theta_n = \bar X_n + \frac1n.$$ In the notation of Proposition 4, $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \mathrm{E}_G[\tau]) = Z_n + \varepsilon_n$ with $Z_n = \sqrt{n}\,\bar X_n \sim N(0, 1)$ (so $\sigma = 1$) and $\varepsilon_n = n^{-1/2}$, a constant; $\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon_n^2] = 1/n$ and $\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon_n^2]/n^{-1/2} = n^{-1/2} \to 0$, so the hypothesis $\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2] = o(n^{-1/2})$ of Proposition 4 holds. By Definition 2, $\theta_{F_n} = \max(-1, \min(1, \hat\theta_n))$. Fix $n = 25$: $\tilde\theta = Z/5$ with $Z \sim N(0, 1)$, and $\hat\theta = Z/5 + \tfrac1{25}$.

Corrected argument in full. Here $n=1,2,\ldots$, each $\hat\theta_n$ is a measurable real-valued random variable on the sampling probability space, and every scale sequence $(a_n)$ is deterministic with $a_n\in(0,\infty)$ for every $n\ge1$. Let Assumption 1 hold ($c > 0$, possibly $+\infty$), let $\theta_{F_n}$ be as in Definition 2, so that $\theta_{F_n} = C(\hat\theta_n)$ and $\hat\theta_n - \theta_{F_n} = r(\hat\theta_n)$, and let $\hat\theta_n$ be root-n consistent and asymptotically normal for $\mu = \mathrm{E}_G[\tau]$ (Definition 1). Then: (a) [exact, for every $n$ and every realization] $\hat\theta_n - \theta_{F_n} = 0$ whenever $|\hat\theta_n - \mu| \le c$; hence for every $\eta > 0$ and every $a_n > 0$, $$\{|\hat\theta_n - \theta_{F_n}| > \eta a_n\} \subseteq \{|\hat\theta_n - \mu| > c\} \quad\text{and}\quad \Pr\left(|\hat\theta_n - \theta_{F_n}| > \eta a_n\right) \le \Pr\left(|\hat\theta_n - \mu| > c\right).$$ (b) [consistency] $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \mu) = O_p(1)$, hence $\Pr(|\hat\theta_n - \mu| > b) \to 0$ for every fixed $b > 0$; in particular $\Pr(|\hat\theta_n - \mu| > c) \to 0$. Since $r$ is 1-Lipschitz, $\mathrm E[r(\hat\theta)^2]\le2\mathrm E[r(\tilde\theta)^2]+2\mathrm E[\varepsilon^2]/n$. Also $r(\tilde\theta)^2\le(\tilde\theta-\mu)^4/c^2$, so the Gaussian fourth moment gives $\mathrm E[r(\hat\theta)^2]\le6\sigma^4/(c^2n^2)+2\mathrm E[\varepsilon^2]/n=o(n^{-1})$. If $c=+\infty$, both errors are identically zero.”]
Corrected argument in full. Let Assumption 1 hold with $c$ finite, $\mu = \mathrm{E}_G[\tau]$, $C(x) = \min(\mu + c, \max(\mu - c, x))$ and $r(x) = x - C(x)$, so that $\theta_{F_n} = C(\hat\theta_n)$ (Definition 2) and $\hat\theta_n - \theta_{F_n} = r(\hat\theta_n)$. Suppose that for each $n$, $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \mu) = Z_n + \varepsilon_n$ with $Z_n \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$, $0 < \sigma^2 < \infty$, and $\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon_n^2] < \infty$; no independence between $Z_n$ and $\varepsilon_n$ is assumed. Write $\tilde\theta_n = \mu + Z_n/\sqrt{n} \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$, so that $\hat\theta_n = \tilde\theta_n + \varepsilon_n/\sqrt{n}$. Then for every $n \ge 1$: (a) $r$ and $C$ are 1-Lipschitz: $|r(x) - r(y)| \le |x - y|$ and $|C(x) - C(y)| \le |x - y|$ for all real $x, y$. (b) $|r(\hat\theta_n)| \le |r(\tilde\theta_n)| + |\varepsilon_n|/\sqrt{n}$, hence $$\mathrm{E}\left[(\hat\theta_n - \theta_{F_n})^2\right] \le 2\,\mathrm{E}\left[r(\tilde\theta_n)^2\right] + \frac{2\,\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon_n^2]}{n}.$$ (c) $r(\tilde\theta_n)^2 = \left(|\tilde\theta_n - \mu| - c\right)_+^2 \le (\tilde\theta_n - \mu)^2\,\mathbf{1}\{|\tilde\theta_n - \mu| > c\} \le (\tilde\theta_n - \mu)^4/c^2$, and $\mathrm{E}[(\tilde\theta_n - \mu)^4] = 3\sigma^4/n^2$. [PDF p. 2, last paragraph] “Our results can be generalized to stronger claims straightforwardly. When a regularity condition is imposed on the rate of convergence of $\hat\theta$ to normality, a stronger result can be obtained about the rate of mean square convergence.”
[PDF p. 3] “Proposition 4: Suppose that Assumption 1 holds and $\hat\theta$ obeys $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \mathrm{E}_G[\tau]) = N(0, \sigma^2) + \varepsilon$, where $\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2] = o(n^{-1/2})$. Then $\mathrm{E}[(\hat\theta - \theta_{F_n})^2] = o(n^{-1})$.”
[Proof as printed: PDF p. 3] “Proof: We will show that the mean square error of $(\tilde\theta - \theta_{F_n})$ converges to zero sufficiently quickly, implying that the rate of convergence of $\hat\theta$ is at worst governed by the mean square error bound ensured by $\varepsilon$’s convergence rate. To obtain the rate of convergence of the mean square error of $\tilde\theta$, we integrate over its squared deviation from the target parameter. Within $c$ of $\mathrm{E}_G[\tau]$, the squared deviation is zero, thus we need only integrate over the squared deviation over the tails of the normal distribution. To ease calculations, we obtain an upper bound by integrating over the squared deviation from $\mathrm{E}_G[\tau]$, rather than from $\theta_{F_n}$: $$\mathrm{E}_G[(\tilde\theta - \theta_{F_n})^2] \le 2\int_c^\infty x^2 \frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{x^2 n}{2\sigma^2}} = c\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\frac{e^{-\frac{c^2 n}{2\sigma^2}}}{\sqrt{n}} + 2\sigma^2\frac{\Phi\left(\frac{-c\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\right)}{n} = o(n^{-1}).$$ Since $\mathrm{E}[(\tilde\theta - \theta_{F_n})^2] = o(n^{-1})$ and $n^{-1/2}\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2] = o(n^{-1})$, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality ensures that $\mathrm{E}[(\hat\theta - \theta_{F_n})^2] = o(n^{-1}) + o(n^{-1}) = o(n^{-1})$.”
